The key difference between nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) that explains why R3P=O exists but R3N=O doesn't is related to their atomic size and electronic structure.

Nitrogen is a second-period element with only the 2s and 2p orbitals available for bonding. It cannot expand its octet because it lacks accessible d orbitals. This means nitrogen is generally limited to forming a maximum of 4 bonds (3 single bonds and 1 double bond, or 4 single bonds with a formal charge).

Phosphorus, being a third-period element, has access to 3d orbitals, which allows it to expand its octet and form more than 4 bonds. This is why phosphorus can accommodate the 5 bonds needed in R3P=O (3 bonds to R groups plus a double bond to oxygen).

The fundamental difference is the atomic radius - phosphorus is significantly larger than nitrogen, which allows it to accommodate more ligands and utilize its d orbitals for hypervalent compounds.
